claim: Migraine is estimated to affect 14% of the global population, making it the third most prevalent disease worldwide.
source: Migraine is an extremely common neurological disorder that is estimated to affect 14% of the global population, making it the third most prevalent disease worldwide (Global Burden of Disease Study 2013 Collaborators, 2015; GBD 2016 Disease and Injury Incidence and Prevalence Collaborators, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Global Burden of Disease studies

claim: Chronic migraine is defined as having more than 15 headache days a month.
source: One particularly debilitating subset of migraine patients are those with chronic migraine, which is defined as having more than 15 headache days a month (Headache Classification Committee of the International Headache Society (IHS), 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to International Headache Society classification

claim: Migraine therapies are often only partially effective or are poorly tolerated.
source: Despite its high prevalence, migraine therapies are often only partially effective or are poorly tolerated, creating a need for better pharmacotherapies (Ford et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ford et al., 2017

claim: Antibodies and antagonists against calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and CGRP receptor demonstrate effectiveness as targeted migraine therapeutics.
source: Recent clinical success of antibodies and antagonists against calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) and CGRP receptor demonstrate the effectiveness of targeted migraine therapeutics.
evidence: Statement about clinical success of CGRP-targeting therapies

claim: HDAC6 is primarily expressed in the cytosol due to its cytoplasmic retention signal.
source: Due to its cytoplasmic retention signal, HDAC6 is primarily expressed in the cytosol (Valenzuela-Fernández et al., 2008), and one of its primary targets for deacetylation is α-tubulin (Valenzuela-Fernández et al., 2008; d'Ydewalle et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Valenzuela-Fernández et al., 2008 and d'Ydewalle et al., 2012

claim: One of HDAC6's primary targets for deacetylation is α-tubulin.
source: Due to its cytoplasmic retention signal, HDAC6 is primarily expressed in the cytosol (Valenzuela-Fernández et al., 2008), and one of its primary targets for deacetylation is α-tubulin (Valenzuela-Fernández et al., 2008; d'Ydewalle et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Valenzuela-Fernández et al., 2008 and d'Ydewalle et al., 2012

claim: Tubulin acetylation is associated with increased flexibility and stability of microtubules.
source: Tubulin acetylation is associated with increased flexibility and stability of microtubules (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2017

claim: Deacetylated microtubules are more fragile and prone to breakage or increased cycling between assembly and disassembly.
source: In contrast, deacetylated microtubules are more fragile and prone to breakage or increased cycling between assembly and disassembly (Xu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2017

claim: Changes in cellular structure such as alterations in dendritic spine density have been implicated in disease chronicity.
source: Importantly, changes in cellular structure such as alterations in dendritic spine density, have been implicated in disease chronicity (Jochems et al., 2015; Forrest et al., 2018; Singh et al., 2018; Nestler and Lüscher, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on cellular structure and disease chronicity

claim: NTG induced severe and sustained cephalic allodynia as measured by von Frey hair stimulation of the periorbital region as compared to vehicle animals.
source: NTG induced severe and sustained cephalic allodynia as measured by von Frey hair stimulation of the periorbital region as compared to vehicle animals on the same day (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Chronic NTG treatment produced a dramatic decrease in neuronal complexity in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis.
source: We observed a dramatic decrease in neuronal complexity after NTG treatment (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Neurons of chronic NTG-treated mice had significantly fewer branch points.
source: Neurons of chronic NTG-treated mice had significantly fewer branch points (Figure 1E), and shorter neurites resulting in decreased overall length of the neurons (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: Neurons of chronic NTG-treated mice had shorter neurites resulting in decreased overall length of the neurons.
source: Neurons of chronic NTG-treated mice had significantly fewer branch points (Figure 1E), and shorter neurites resulting in decreased overall length of the neurons (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Sholl Analysis showed a significant decrease in the number of intersections following NTG treatment.
source: Further examination of the complexity of the neurons using Sholl Analysis, showed a significant decrease in the number of intersections following NTG treatment (Figure 1G–I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G-I

claim: Neurons from NTG-treated mice in the somatosensory cortex had fewer branch points, were shorter in length, and had fewer intersections.
source: We examined the somatosensory cortex (SCx) and periaqueductal gray (PAG) of these mice and found similar results, where neurons from NTG-treated mice had fewer branch points, were shorter in length, and had fewer intersections (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D and E–H, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D

claim: Neurons from NTG-treated mice in the periaqueductal gray had fewer branch points, were shorter in length, and had fewer intersections.
source: We examined the somatosensory cortex (SCx) and periaqueductal gray (PAG) of these mice and found similar results, where neurons from NTG-treated mice had fewer branch points, were shorter in length, and had fewer intersections (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D and E–H, respectively).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E–H

claim: No alteration in number of branches, total neuron length, or Sholl analysis was found in the nucleus accumbens shell following NTG treatment.
source: To ensure that this effect was associated with migraine-pain processing and not a non-specific effect of NTG we also analyzed neuronal complexity in the nucleus accumbens shell (NAc), a region more commonly associated with reward, and found no alteration in number of branches, total neuron length, or Sholl analysis for cells in this region (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–L).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I–L

claim: No differences in NTG versus vehicle controls in number of branches, total neuron length, or Sholl analysis were observed in the dorsal horn of the lumbar and cervical spinal cord.
source: Furthermore, we also examined the dorsal horn of the lumbar and cervical spinal cord, important sites for pain processing in the peripheral nervous system. No differences in NTG versus vehicle controls in number of branches, total neuron length, or Sholl analysis were observed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1M–T).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1M–T

claim: ACY-738 treatment resulted in a significant increase in the ratio of acetylated α-tubulin to total tubulin within the trigeminal ganglia, TNC, SCx, NAc, and spinal cord.
source: ACY-738 treatment resulted in a significant increase in the ratio of acetylated α-tubulin to total tubulin within the trigeminal ganglia (TG), TNC, SCx, NAc, and spinal cord (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Treatment with ACY-738 led to a significant increase in branch points, combined neurite length, and number of intersections in both chronic vehicle and NTG groups.
source: In contrast, treatment with ACY-738 led to a significant increase in these measures in both chronic vehicle and NTG groups (Figure 2A–F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A–F

claim: ACY-738 significantly reversed cephalic allodynia in NTG treated mice for up to 24 hr post-injection.
source: ACY-738 significantly reversed cephalic allodynia in NTG treated mice for up to 24 hr post-injection.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 3A

claim: Mechanical responses in ACY-738 treated animals not treated with NTG were unaffected.
source: Mechanical responses in ACY-738 treated animals, not treated with NTG were unaffected (Figure 3A, VEH-ACY), suggesting that augmentation of neuronal complexity by HDAC6 inhibitor in a pain-free animal does not alter endogenous pain processing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A

claim: The half-life of ACY-738 is only 12 min.
source: Interestingly, the half-life of ACY-738 is only 12 min (Jochems et al., 2014), thus short-term inhibition of HDAC6 still produced long-lasting behavioral and cytoarchitectural changes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Jochems et al., 2014

claim: At 24 hr post-ACY-738, NTG-Veh animals continued to show significantly fewer branch points as compared to the Veh-Veh controls.
source: At 24 hr post-ACY-738, NTG-Veh animals continued to show significantly fewer branch points as compared to the Veh-Veh controls (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C

claim: At 24 hr post-ACY-738, the NTG-ACY group had a significantly higher number of branches compared to NTG-Veh.
source: In contrast, the NTG-ACY group had a significantly higher number of branches compared to NTG-Veh.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 3C

claim: At 48 hr post-ACY-738, the number of branch points were significantly lower in both the NTG-vehicle and NTG-ACY groups compared to VEH-VEH controls.
source: At 48 hr post-ACY-738 we observed that compared to the VEH-VEH controls, the number of branch points were now significantly lower in both the NTG-vehicle and NTG-ACY groups (Figure 3F); and similar results were observed for total neuronal length (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F

claim: The pan-HDAC inhibitor trichostatin A (TSA) significantly reversed chronic NTG-induced allodynia.
source: We first tested two pan-HDAC inhibitors: the well-characterized inhibitor trichostatin A (TSA, Figure 4A); and a novel brain-penetrant pan-HDAC inhibitor, RN-73 (Abdelkarim et al., 2017; Figure 4B). Both significantly reversed chronic NTG-induced allodynia, albeit for a much shorter duration than ACY-738.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A

claim: The novel brain-penetrant pan-HDAC inhibitor RN-73 significantly reversed chronic NTG-induced allodynia.
source: We first tested two pan-HDAC inhibitors: the well-characterized inhibitor trichostatin A (TSA, Figure 4A); and a novel brain-penetrant pan-HDAC inhibitor, RN-73 (Abdelkarim et al., 2017; Figure 4B). Both significantly reversed chronic NTG-induced allodynia, albeit for a much shorter duration than ACY-738.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The Class I, HDAC1 and 2 selective inhibitor ASV-85 did not produce any change in NTG-induced chronic allodynia relative to vehicle controls.
source: In contrast, when we tested the Class I, HDAC1 and 2 selective inhibitor, ASV-85 (Supplementary file 1), we did not observe any change in NTG-induced chronic allodynia relative to vehicle controls (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Concurrent treatment with ACY-738 prevented the development of NTG-induced allodynia.
source: As seen previously, chronic NTG resulted in the development of a chronic allodynia (Figure 4D, VEH-NTG vs VEH-VEH); and concurrent treatment with ACY-738 prevented the development of this allodynia (VEH-NTG vs ACY-NTG).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D

claim: HDAC6 transcripts are abundantly expressed in trigeminal ganglia, trigeminal nucleus caudalis, and somatosensory cortex.
source: In situ hybridization using RNAScope and immunohistochemical analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B) revealed abundant expression of HDAC6 transcripts in TG, TNC, and SCx.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Chronic NTG treatment increased HDAC6 expression in the trigeminal ganglia.
source: Gene expression analysis revealed that, of these regions, chronic NTG treatment increased HDAC6 expression in the TG (Figure 4-figure supplement 1C), which are the first-order cells regulating cephalic pain processing.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4-figure supplement 1C

claim: Pretreatment with ACY-738 resulted in significantly fewer CSD events relative to vehicle controls.
source: Pretreatment with ACY-738 resulted in significantly fewer CSD events relative to vehicle controls (Figure 5D), indicating that HDAC6 inhibition is also effective in this mechanistically separate migraine model.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D

claim: CSD evoked a significant decrease in branch points and total length of neurons in the somatosensory cortex.
source: In the somatosensory cortex, CSD evoked a significant decrease in branch points (Figure 6C) and total length of neurons (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and 6D

claim: CSD resulted in a significant reduction in the number of branches in neurons of the TNC.
source: In addition, CSD also resulted in a significant reduction in the number of branches in neurons of the TNC (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), a region that is known to be activated following CSD events (Zhang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1

claim: ACY-738 increased neuronal complexity in the cortex in both sham and CSD groups.
source: In contrast, ACY-738 increased neuronal complexity in the cortex in both sham and CSD groups.
evidence: Supported by experimental data described in the text and shown in Figure 6

claim: Sholl analysis demonstrated a dramatic decrease in neuronal complexity after CSD, while ACY-738 treatment had the opposite effect.
source: Sholl analysis demonstrated a dramatic decrease in neuronal complexity after CSD, while ACY-738 treatment had the opposite effect (Figure 6E–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E–G

claim: Olcegepant significantly inhibited NTG-induced cephalic allodynia.
source: Olcegepant significantly inhibited NTG-induced cephalic allodynia (Figure 7B), similar to previously published reports (Christensen et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and citation to Christensen et al., 2019

claim: Chronic NTG treatment decreased the number of branch points, combined neurite length, and number of intersections in the TNC.
source: As was observed previously, chronic NTG treatment decreased the number of branch points (Figure 7D), combined neurite length (Figure 7E), and number of intersections using Sholl analysis (Figure 7F–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D, 7E, and 7F–H

claim: Olcegepant treatment restored neuronal complexity induced by chronic NTG.
source: Interestingly, olcegepant treatment restored neuronal complexity induced by chronic NTG, but had no effect in chronic vehicle-treated mice (Figure 7C–H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C–H

claim: NTG is a known human migraine trigger and is used as a human experimental model of migraine.
source: NTG is a known human migraine trigger and is used as a human experimental model of migraine (Schytz et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schytz et al., 2010

claim: Similar to humans, NTG produces a delayed allodynia in mice.
source: Similar to humans, NTG produces a delayed allodynia in mice (Bates et al., 2010), as well as photophobia and altered meningeal blood flow (Markovics et al., 2012; Greco et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bates et al., 2010, Markovics et al., 2012, and Greco et al., 2011

claim: Chronic intermittent administration of NTG is used to model chronic migraine.
source: Chronic intermittent administration of NTG is used to model chronic migraine (Pradhan et al., 2014a; Farajdokht et al., 2018; Long et al., 2018; Christensen et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies using chronic NTG model

claim: NTG-induced hypersensitivity in mice is inhibited by migraine-specific medications, such as sumatriptan and CGRP targeting drugs.
source: However, NTG-induced hypersensitivity in mice is inhibited by migraine-specific medications, such as sumatriptan (Bates et al., 2010; Pradhan et al., 2014a; Pradhan et al., 2014b) and CGRP targeting drugs (Christensen et al., 2019), as well as the migraine preventives propranolol and topiramate (Tipton et al., 2016; Greco et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies showing efficacy of migraine medications in NTG model

claim: Mice with human migraine gene mutations are more sensitive to NTG.
source: Further, mice with human migraine gene mutations are more sensitive to NTG (Brennan et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brennan et al., 2013

claim: Systemic administration of NTG causes cellular activation throughout nociceptive pathways including in the TNC and brainstem.
source: Systemic administration of NTG also causes cellular activation throughout nociceptive pathways including in the TNC and brainstem (Tassorelli and Joseph, 1995a; Tassorelli and Joseph, 1995b; Ramachandran et al., 2012; Greco et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies showing NTG-induced cellular activation

claim: Previous studies have shown an increase in TNC activity in headache models.
source: Previous studies have shown an increase in TNC activity in headache models (Oshinsky and Luo, 2006; Akerman et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Oshinsky and Luo, 2006 and Akerman et al., 2013

claim: CSD is thought to be the electrophysiological correlate of migraine aura.
source: CSD is thought to underlie migraine aura and reflects changes in cortical excitability associated with the migraine brain state (Charles and Baca, 2013; Brennan and Pietrobon, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Charles and Baca, 2013 and Brennan and Pietrobon, 2018

claim: Neuronal swelling and dendritic beading were observed following spreading depression events.
source: Neuronal swelling (Takano et al., 2007) and dendritic beading (Steffensen et al., 2015) were observed following spreading depression events.
evidence: Supported by citations to Takano et al., 2007 and Steffensen et al., 2015

claim: CSD resulted in alterations in dendritic structure and volumetric changes.
source: CSD also resulted in alterations in dendritic structure (Takano et al., 2007; Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2015) and volumetric changes (Takano et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Takano et al., 2007 and Eikermann-Haerter et al., 2015

claim: Steffensen et al. showed decreased microtubule presence in dendrites following spreading depression in hippocampal slices.
source: Further, Steffensen et al. showed decreased microtubule presence in dendrites following spreading depression in hippocampal slices, again implying alterations in cytoarchitectural dynamics (Steffensen et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Steffensen et al., 2015

claim: Microtubules have been shown to disassemble in response to increased intracellular calcium.
source: Microtubules have been shown to disassemble in response to increased intracellular calcium (Schliwa et al., 1981); and the increased calcium influx induced by spreading depolarization (Basarsky et al., 1998) may facilitate this breakdown.
evidence: Supported by citations to Schliwa et al., 1981 and Basarsky et al., 1998

claim: CSD waves pass through the neuron in phases, from apical dendrites, to somatodendritic sites, and finally to proximal dendrites.
source: In addition, CSD waves pass through the neuron in phases, from apical dendrites, to somatodendritic sites, and finally to proximal dendrites (Pietrobon and Moskowitz, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pietrobon and Moskowitz, 2014

claim: Multiple reports indicate that CSD can activate the trigeminovascular complex, and evoke cephalic allodynia in rodents.
source: Furthermore, multiple reports indicate that CSD can activate the trigeminovascular complex, and evoke cephalic allodynia in rodents (Bolay et al., 2002; Fioravanti et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2012; Noseda and Burstein, 2013; Melo-Carrillo et al., 2017; Filiz et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies showing CSD effects on trigeminovascular system

claim: Knockout of the α-tubulin acetylating enzyme, α-TAT1, in peripheral sensory neurons results in profound deficits in touch.
source: Knockout of the α-tubulin acetylating enzyme, α-TAT1, in peripheral sensory neurons results in profound deficits in touch (Morley et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Morley et al., 2016

claim: Mouse models of CMT reveal deficits in mitochondrial transport in the dorsal root ganglia due to reduced α-tubulin acetylation, and HDAC6 inhibition ameliorate CMT-associated symptoms.
source: Mouse models of CMT reveal deficits in mitochondrial transport in the dorsal root ganglia (DRG) due to reduced α-tubulin acetylation, and HDAC6 inhibition ameliorate CMT-associated symptoms (d'Ydewalle et al., 2011; Benoy et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to d'Ydewalle et al., 2011 and Benoy et al., 2018

claim: Other groups using ACY-738 or other HDAC6 inhibitors did not observe general disruption in mechanical or temperature sensitivity with HDAC6 inhibition.
source: Other groups using ACY-738 or other HDAC6 inhibitors also did not observe general disruption in mechanical or temperature sensitivity with HDAC6 inhibition (Krukowski et al., 2017; Van Helleputte et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2019; Sakloth et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies showing no general sensory disruption with HDAC6 inhibition

claim: Constitutive knockout of HDAC6 produces viable offspring with few phenotypic changes.
source: Additionally, constitutive knockout of HDAC6 produces viable offspring with few phenotypic changes (Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2008

claim: A mouse model of chronic constriction injury of the sciatic nerve reduced neurite length in GABA neurons within lamina II of the spinal cord.
source: A mouse model of chronic constriction injury of the sciatic nerve reduced neurite length in GABA neurons within lamina II of the spinal cord (Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2018

claim: Following spared nerve injury, there were decreases in the number of branches and neurite length of hippocampal neurons but increases in spinal dorsal horn neurons.
source: Another group observed that following spared nerve injury, there were decreases in the number of branches and neurite length of hippocampal neurons but increases in spinal dorsal horn neurons (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2017

claim: HDAC6 inhibitors were shown to effectively reduce chemotherapy-induced allodynia following treatment with vincristine or cisplatin in mice.
source: HDAC6 inhibitors have been studied in other models of pain. They were shown to effectively reduce chemotherapy-induced allodynia following treatment with vincristine (Van Helleputte et al., 2018) or cisplatin (Krukowski et al., 2017) in mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to Van Helleputte et al., 2018 and Krukowski et al., 2017

claim: Chemotherapy blunted mitochondrial transport in sensory neurons, an effect that was restored by HDAC6 inhibition.
source: In addition, both groups found that chemotherapy blunted mitochondrial transport in sensory neurons, an effect that was restored by HDAC6 inhibition.
evidence: Supported by references to studies on chemotherapy and HDAC6 inhibition

claim: HDAC6 inhibitors were effective in models of inflammatory and neuropathic pain.
source: Another study also found that HDAC6 inhibitors were effective in models of inflammatory and neuropathic pain (Sakloth et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sakloth et al., 2020

claim: HDAC6 deacetylates Hsp90, which plays an important role in glucocorticoid receptor maturation and adaptation to stress.
source: HDAC6 deacetylates Hsp90, which plays an important role in glucocorticoid receptor maturation and adaptation to stress (Kovacs et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kovacs et al., 2005

claim: In social defeat stress, HDAC6 knockout or inhibition decreased Hsp90-glucocorticoid receptor interaction and subsequent glucocorticoid signaling, thus encouraging resilience.
source: A previous study showed that in social defeat stress HDAC6 knockout or inhibition decreased Hsp90-glucocorticoid receptor interaction and subsequent glucocorticoid signaling, thus encouraging resilience (Espallergues et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Espallergues et al., 2012

claim: HDAC6 inhibitors show antidepressant-like effects.
source: In line with these findings, HDAC6 inhibitors also show antidepressant-like effects (Covington et al., 2009; Jochems et al., 2014), and membrane-associated acetylated tubulin is decreased in humans with depression (Singh et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Covington et al., 2009 and Jochems et al., 2014

claim: Membrane-associated acetylated tubulin is decreased in humans with depression.
source: In line with these findings, HDAC6 inhibitors also show antidepressant-like effects (Covington et al., 2009; Jochems et al., 2014), and membrane-associated acetylated tubulin is decreased in humans with depression (Singh et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Singh et al., 2020

claim: HDAC6 directly deacetylates cortactin, a protein that regulates actin-dependent cell motility.
source: Further, HDAC6 also directly deacetylates cortactin, a protein that regulates actin-dependent cell motility (Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2007

claim: Olcegepant was previously shown to poorly cross the blood brain barrier.
source: Olcegepant was previously shown to poorly cross the blood brain barrier; and it may result in cytoarchitectural changes in the central nervous system by blocking nociceptive signals from the periphery, resulting in upstream changes in the TNC and other central regions.
evidence: Statement about olcegepant's blood-brain barrier penetration

claim: Human imaging studies reveal decreased cortical thickness in migraine patients.
source: Human imaging studies reveal decreased cortical thickness (Magon et al., 2019), and gray matter reductions in the insula, anterior cingulate cortex, and amygdala of migraine patients (Valfrè et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Magon et al., 2019 and Valfrè et al., 2008

claim: Gray matter reductions in the insula, anterior cingulate cortex, and amygdala are observed in migraine patients.
source: Human imaging studies reveal decreased cortical thickness (Magon et al., 2019), and gray matter reductions in the insula, anterior cingulate cortex, and amygdala of migraine patients (Valfrè et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Valfrè et al., 2008

claim: A significant correlation was observed between gray matter reduction in anterior cingulate cortex and frequency of migraine attacks.
source: Interestingly, a significant correlation was observed between gray matter reduction in anterior cingulate cortex and frequency of migraine attacks (Valfrè et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Valfrè et al., 2008

claim: Decreased neuronal complexity may be a feature that maintains the chronic migraine state.
source: These results suggest that decreased neuronal complexity may be a feature that maintains the chronic migraine state; a previously undiscovered phenomenon.
evidence: Inferred from experimental findings showing decreased neuronal complexity in chronic migraine models

claim: Restoration of neuronal complexity correlates with decreased allodynia.
source: These data further strengthen the correlation between cytoarchitectural complexity and decreased allodynia, as at both 4 and 24 hr post-injection ACY-738 has anti-allodynic effects.
evidence: Inferred from temporal correlation between restored neuronal complexity and anti-allodynic effects

claim: The anti-allodynic effects of ACY-378 correspond with the times at which it also restores neuronal complexity.
source: Taken together, these data show that the anti-allodynic effects of ACY-378 correspond with the times at which it also restores neuronal complexity.
evidence: Inferred from temporal correlation between behavioral and cytoarchitectural effects

claim: Chronic migraine-associated pain can be blocked specifically by HDCA6 inhibition, and this effect is not likely due to acetylation of histones in the cell nucleus.
source: These data further support our finding that chronic migraine-associated pain can be blocked specifically by HDCA6 inhibition, and that this effect is not likely due to acetylation of histones in the cell nucleus.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of HDAC6-selective inhibitor effects versus Class I HDAC inhibitor effects

claim: Decreased neuronal flexibility could encourage the strengthening of excitatory synapses and/or prevent the formation of inhibitory synapses.
source: For example, decreased neuronal flexibility could encourage the strengthening of excitatory synapses and/or prevent the formation of inhibitory synapses, as the cell is in a more fixed state.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about how decreased neuronal complexity might affect synaptic function

claim: HDAC6 inhibition could attenuate CSD through increased tubulin acetylation, thus counteracting microtubule disassembly produced by CSD events.
source: One way in which HDAC6 inhibitors could attenuate CSD is through increased tubulin acetylation, thus counteracting microtubule disassembly produced by CSD events.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about mechanism of HDAC6 inhibitor effects on CSD

claim: HDAC6 inhibition could redistribute or disturb the phasic movement of CSD events, which may decrease and/or elongate CSD events.
source: Along with preventing the dendritic alterations that occur in response to calcium influx, it is possible that HDAC6 inhibition could redistribute or disturb the phasic movement of CSD events, which may decrease and/or elongate CSD events.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms of HDAC6 inhibitor effects on CSD

claim: An increase in CGRP could result in altered microtubule assembly.
source: Previous studies have shown that activation of various Gα subunits, including αi, αo, αs, can inhibit microtubule assembly (Roychowdhury et al., 1999). Therefore, it is possible that an increase in CGRP, which was found to be present following NTG (Greco et al., 2018; Moye et al., 2021), could result in altered microtubule assembly.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on known G protein effects and CGRP increases after NTG

claim: Inhibition of the CGRP receptor could reverse altered microtubule assembly allowing for elaboration of microtubules.
source: Inhibition of the CGRP receptor could therefore reverse this process allowing for elaboration of microtubules.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about mechanism of CGRP receptor antagonist effects

claim: Olcegepant may result in cytoarchitectural changes in the central nervous system by blocking nociceptive signals from the periphery, resulting in upstream changes in the TNC and other central regions.
source: Olcegepant was previously shown to poorly cross the blood brain barrier; and it may result in cytoarchitectural changes in the central nervous system by blocking nociceptive signals from the periphery, resulting in upstream changes in the TNC and other central regions.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about mechanism of olcegepant's central effects given poor BBB penetration

claim: Recovered neuronal complexity is a marker of effective migraine medication.
source: This study suggests a possible mechanism in which recovered neuronal complexity is a marker of effective migraine medication.
evidence: Inferred from correlation between neuronal complexity restoration and anti-migraine effects of both HDAC6 inhibitor and CGRP antagonist

claim: Structural changes in migraine patients could reflect decreased neuronal complexity in combination with other factors.
source: Human imaging studies reveal decreased cortical thickness (Magon et al., 2019), and gray matter reductions in the insula, anterior cingulate cortex, and amygdala of migraine patients (Valfrè et al., 2008). Interestingly, a significant correlation was observed between gray matter reduction in anterior cingulate cortex and frequency of migraine attacks (Valfrè et al., 2008). These structural changes could reflect decreased neuronal complexity in combination with other factors.
evidence: Speculative reasoning connecting human imaging findings to experimental observations of decreased neuronal complexity

claim: HDAC6 inhibitors may restore cellular adaptations induced by chronic disease states but may not otherwise affect healthy physiological function.
source: Our results suggest that HDAC6 inhibitors may restore cellular adaptations induced by chronic disease states but may not otherwise affect healthy physiological function; and such compounds could contribute to the migraine therapeutic armamentarium.
evidence: Inferred from observations that HDAC6 inhibitors reverse pathological changes without affecting normal sensory function
